title: Delaware Winter Camps on Kentucky Ground
summary: Lenape (Delaware) bands used Kentucky as seasonal hunting country, slipping south from Ohio villages in fall and winter to hunt deer and bear.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Lenape](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lenape), or Delaware, were an eastern people. Their towns once stood along the Delaware River and the Atlantic coast. Colonial land deals pushed them out. The worst was Pennsylvania's 1737 [Walking Purchase](https://grokipedia.com/page/Walking_Purchase), when colony agents used trained runners to "walk off" a huge tract that was supposed to measure a day and a half on foot. By the 1750s many Lenape had moved west to the Ohio country.

From villages north of the Ohio, Lenape bands used Kentucky as hunting country. They often came alongside Shawnee, Mingo, Miami, and Wyandot hunters. In the fall and winter, small family parties slipped south across the river to hunt deer, elk, bear, and buffalo. They set up light camps of bark or hides, dried meat, and took skins to trade. In the spring they went home.

That pattern left little behind for later settlers to see. Anglo long hunters who found old fires and empty camps often took the land as wild and unclaimed. It was not. It was a shared hunting ground, used by many nations and claimed by several. None of the sources cited here documents a specific Delaware camp site in Kentucky, so this story does not name one.

By the 1770s, things changed. Surveyors, hunters, and then settlers poured into Kentucky after the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](/stories/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768/). Hunting parties found the game shrinking and strangers on the land. More and more, hunts became raids. Lenape warriors joined the war against Kentucky settlers in the Revolution, including the [1780 raids on Ruddle's and Martin's stations](/stories/delaware-lenape-in-the-1780-kentucky-raids/).

The "dark and bloody ground" legend grew out of that time. [John Filson](/people/#john-filson) and other early writers made Kentucky sound like an empty wilderness where nations only came to fight. Archaeologist A. Gwynn Henderson has shown that the truth is more ordinary: Native people used Kentucky all the time, for hunting, salt, and travel. The [Mingo camps south of the Ohio](/stories/mingo-camps-south-of-the-ohio/) are part of the same story.

## Kentucky today

The Lenape live on in Oklahoma as the [Delaware Nation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Delaware_Nation) at Anadarko and the Delaware Tribe of Indians at Bartlesville. In Kentucky, their trace is mostly in the old hunting country itself.
Source: [A. Gwynn Henderson, "Dispelling the Myth: Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century Indian Life in Kentucky," Register of the Kentucky Historical Society 90, no. 1 (1992) (PDF)](https://preservationkentucky.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Dispelling-the-Myth-17th-18th-Century-Indian-Life-in-KY.pdf)
Source: [History (Delaware Nation, Anadarko, Oklahoma)](https://www.delawarenation-nsn.gov/history/)
